Analyzing Uncertainty Quantification in Statistical
and Deep Learning Models for Probabilistic
Electricity Price Forecasting
ANDREAS LEBEDEV 1
 , ABHINAV DAS 2
 , SVEN PAPPERT 3
 , and STEPHAN SCHLÜTER 1
1Institute of Energy Engineering and Energy Economics, Ulm University of Applied Sciences, Prittwitzstrasse 10, 89075 Ulm, Germany (e-mail:
andreaslebedev@outlook.de; Stephan.Schlueter@thu.de)
2Faculty of Mathematics and Economics, Ulm University, Helmholtzstrasse 20, 89081 Ulm, Germany (e-mail: abhinav.das@uni-ulm.de)
3Department of Statistics, TU Dortmund University, V ogelpothsweg 78, 44227 Dortmund, Germany (e-mail: pappert@mail.statistik.tu-dortmund.de)

ABSTRACTPrecise probabilistic forecasts are fundamental for energy risk management, and there is a
wide range of both statistical and machine learning models for this purpose. Inherent to these probabilistic
models is some form of uncertainty quantification. However, most models do not capture the full extent of
uncertainty, which arises not only from the data itself but also from model and distributional choices. In this
study, we examine uncertainty quantification in state-of-the-art statistical and deep learning probabilistic
forecasting models for electricity price forecasting in the German market. In particular, we consider
distributional deep neural networks (DDNNs) and augment them with an ensemble approach, Monte Carlo
(MC) dropout, LASSO-estimated autoregressive (LEAR), and conformal prediction to account for model
uncertainty. Additionally, we consider the eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) approach combined with
quantile regression averaging (QRA), generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (GARCH),
and conformal prediction. Across a range of performance metrics, we find that the XGBoost-based models
perform well in terms of probabilistic forecasting, irrespective of the uncertainty quantification method.
Furthermore, we find that DDNNs benefit from incorporating both data and model uncertainty, improving
both point and probabilistic forecasting. Uncertainty itself appears to be best captured by the models using
conformal prediction. Overall, our extensive study shows that all models under consideration perform com-
petitively. However, their relative performance depends on the choice of metrics for point and probabilistic
forecasting.
INDEX TERMSBayesian methods, deep learning, electricity price forecasting, ensemble learning, interval
forecasting, machine learning, Monte Carlo methods, power markets, probabilistic forecasting, uncertainty
quantification
I. INTRODUCTION
T
HE energy industry has been in turmoil lately. On the
positive side, we see a considerable increase in renew-
able energy, leading to a reduced carbon footprint of power
production. However, this comes with a drawback, as re-
newable power can be highly fluctuating, which leads to
increased production risk and larger price volatility in turn.
This volatility is further amplified by various geopolitical
developments in 2025, such as the ongoing war in Ukraine.
Risk management for power utilities, energy-related compa-
nies, and governments is becoming not only important but es-
sential. This involves reliable forecasts. In risk management,
probabilistic/interval forecasts are of particular interest, as
point forecasts ignore information about uncertainty arising
from model choice, data, or parameter calibration.
In the electricity price forecasting literature, several authors
have focused on developing (probabilistic) forecasting mod-
els for power prices. See, e.g., [1], [2], and [3] for overviews.
For general overviews of probabilistic/interval forecasting,
see [4] and [5].
Despite various refined models, existing research often ad-
dresses data-related uncertainty, whereas uncertainty arising
from model choice and calibration is often overlooked (see
Section II-A for more details). Including this uncertainty, e.g.,
via ensemble or Bayesian approaches, considerably increases
complexity and computational challenges, and it remains to

be verified whether the additional effort pays off. So far, to the
authors’ best knowledge, there has been no deeper analysis
in electricity price forecasting with regard to this question.
Hence, we propose to compare probabilistic forecasts and
prediction intervals (PIs) generated by distributional deep
learning and statistical models in combination with various
uncertainty quantification methods. In addition, we discuss
which evaluation measure is adequate here. For illustration
and testing purposes, we use historical energy price data
from the German market. These data not only show high
volatility but also multiple structural breaks in the past and
are therefore adequate for thoroughly testing methods for un-
certainty quantification and comparison with forecasts from
other models. In this work, we demonstrate that accounting
for both data and model uncertainty, particularly for deep
learning models, yields significant benefits. As shown in
Section IV, this approach leads to more reliable PIs as well as
improved point forecasts. We also find that statistical models
are highly competitive, even when compared to complex
machine learning models. The main findings are summarized
as follows:
•Uncertainty quantification benefits the performance of
deep distributional neural networks in forecasting Ger-
man electricity prices. Distributional accuracy is in-
creased by up to 7%, and the mean absolute error of
mean forecasts is decreased by up to 7%.
•For linear statistical models, different approaches to un-
certainty quantification (parametric, ensemble or con-
formal) yield comparable results in terms of distribu-
tional accuracy, while conformal prediction captures un-
certainty itself best.
•For the German market, the overall best performing
model is the conformal-prediction XGBoost model.
The article is structured as follows: In Section II, we dis-
cuss state-of-the-art approaches for (probabilistic/interval)
electricity price forecasting from both machine learning and
statistics, commenting on their approaches to quantifying un-
certainty and motivating additional approaches to uncertainty
quantification. In Section III, the data for the case study is
introduced. The forecasting study is presented in Section IV,
where we discuss how models are calibrated and trained (in-
cluding hyperparameter choices), and compare results using
suitable metrics. Before we conclude the article in Section VI,
we discuss our results in Section V.
II. A REVISION OF CONCEPTS FOR FORECASTING AND
UNCERTAINTY QUANTIFICATION
There are various approaches for generating probabilistic
and interval forecasts. First, there are parametric distribution-
based approaches that rely on certain assumptions about the
underlying probability distribution of the data. The PIs are
constructed by estimating the parameters of the (conditional)
distribution and using the corresponding quantiles, as in dis-
tributional deep neural networks (DDNNs) [6]. Then, some
methods directly learn specific aspects of a forecast, e.g.,
direct quantile learning methods such as quantile regression
[7], which do not require distributional assumptions. Finally,
there are model-agnostic approaches such as bootstrapping
[8], historical simulation [9], or conformal prediction [9],
which do not rely on any specific underlying distribution or
regression model. These approaches are applied to already
trained models.
In Section II-A, we first review concepts of uncertainty
quantification. Then we proceed to introduce state-of-the-
art statistical and machine learning models for probabilistic
electricity price forecasting and discuss them in the context
of uncertainty.
A. A FEW NOTES ON UNCERTAINTY
Forecasting intervals are an attempt to quantify and estimate
the uncertainty connected to the behavior of a stochastic
process. However, uncertainty itself needs to be taken into ac-
count when designing or choosing a model for the generation
of PIs.
Generally speaking, uncertainty can be categorized into
two types: aleatoric uncertainty, which describes data-related
uncertainty [10], and epistemic uncertainty, which relates to
model-specific uncertainties [11], [12]. Aleatoric uncertainty
arises from the variability inherent in the input data and
cannot be reduced, not even by collecting more data. Sources
of aleatoric uncertainty include measurement errors or the use
of inherently uncertain input features, such as energy demand
estimates or weather forecasts. Epistemic uncertainty, on the
other hand, arises from uncertainties related to the choice of
model features, such as the general architecture (e.g., using
a linear model to capture nonlinear relationships), the pa-
rameters, and the distributional properties. Especially when
dealing with nonstationary processes and potential structural
breaks, we must address domain-shift uncertainty, which de-
scribes potential differences in the distributional properties of
calibration and test data. Unlike aleatoric uncertainty, epis-
temic uncertainty can be reduced. Key strategies for min-
imizing it include selecting a suitable model architecture,
employing an effective optimization and training process, and
using a well-distributed and representative training dataset.
Ultimately, the resulting overall uncertainty related to the pre-
diction for a specific sample is called predictive uncertainty.
B. STATISTICAL APPROACHES
The standard approach to statistical interval forecasting is to
assume an underlying distribution and obtain the interval by
extracting the corresponding quantiles. The simplest way to
model a distribution is the naive model. The model naively
uses a previous days price as mean forecast. To estimate price
distributions, historical simulation may be applied, relying on
the widely used Gaussian distribution. This involves fitting
distribution parameters to the forecast errors from a selected
dataset. We refer to these models as Naive-HStrain and Naive-
HSval, depending on whether the training or validation set was
used.
With regard to the distribution’s volatility parameters, there
are more complex approaches, such as the generalized au-
2 VOLUME 11, 2023

Lebedevet al.: Preparation of Papers for IEEE Access
toregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (GARCH) model
(see [13]), which models the volatility parametrically, using
an autoregressive model for it. Other parametric approaches
such as copulas, see e.g. [14], might be used as well but are
beyond the scope of this paper. The uncertainty may also be
captured by ensemble methods or conformal prediction.
We consider two sophisticated models for mean forecast-
ing. These models are the LASSO estimated AR model
(LEAR), cf. [15], and the extreme gradient boosting (XG-
Boost), cf. [16]. We augment these two mean-forecasting
models with the following mechanisms to capture uncer-
tainty. 1) applying quantile regression averaging to differ-
ent mean predictions, i.e., XGBoost/LEAR-QRA. LEAR-
QRA was proposed by [2] (see also [6], Sect. 4.3.2), but
the methodology can be translated seamlessly to XGBoost.
2) fitting a GARCH model on the residuals of the XG-
Boost/LEAR model to obtain predictions for the conditional
variance, which together with the conditional mean forecast
parametrizes a conditional distribution. 3) Using conformal
prediction on the mean forecasts of the respective models.
We start by introducing the LEAR and XGBoost models
for mean forecasting. Afterwards, the uncertainty modeling
augmentations are described. The LEAR model for electricity
price forecasting, originally introduced by [15], assumes an
autoregressive model with external regressors for each prod-
uct individually and then estimates the coefficients using a
LASSO penalty (see [17] for the LASSO penalty). For each
product, the model may be written as
yt =β 0 +Y t β+X t γ+ε t ,(1)
where{y t }t∈Z is the time series of interest,Y t =
(yt−1 , . . . ,yt−p)contains past values of{y t }, andX t =
(x1,t−1 , . . . ,x1,t−p 1 , . . . ,xr,t−1 , . . . ,xr,t−p r )contains the past
values of the external regressors. The parameters are esti-
mated by minimizing the LASSO-augmented sum of squares.
If the penalty parameter is chosen correctly, the estimator
will select only the relevant past lags ofy t and the external
regressors. This enhances precision and decreases the vari-
ability of the mean predictions. Potential multicollinearity in
the features is automatically taken care of.
As an alternative to the parametric LEAR model, we consider
a tree based model in conjunction with boosting, i.e. exteme
gradient boosting (XGBoost), cf. [16]. In the XGBoost frame-
work, the idea of using boosting with trees as base learners, as
in [18], is modified to be sparsity aware and computationally
efficient. Problems such as multicollinearity are hence auto-
matically taken care of by the model. Adjusted versions of
XGBoost are used by e.g. [19] and [20] for electricity price
forecasting. While it is structurally based on trees, it relies
heavily in the statistical learning theory like gradient descent,
regularization, etc, and hence we include XGBoost model in
this section. Similar to the LEAR-model, XGBoost produces
mean predictions. We augment the models by different ap-
proaches to capture uncertainty:
For the XGBoost/LEAR-QRA model, different mean pre-
dictions are required. We follow the procedure of [2] and
train the models on different horizons to obtain different
mean forecasts. In totalmmean forecasts are obtained (in
the application, we setm= 4). Then, a quantile regression
with these mean forecasts as regressors is fitted for a range
of percentile in order to generate PIs. To obtain probabilistic
forecasts for an observation from the test data the models
are re-fitted for themhorizons, and the respective mean
predictions are obtained. Afterwards, the mean predictions
are used in conjunction with the fitted quantile regression
coefficients to obtain predictions for a range of percentile.
The collection of the percentiles constitutes the probabilistic
forecast.
The XGBoost/LEAR-GARCH model follows a different ap-
proach. Instead of relying on ensemble-based estimators for
the probabilistic forecast, the conditional variance is pre-
dicted by a GARCH model. Assuming an underlying con-
ditional distribution, the conditional mean (given by the
LEAR prediction) and the conditional variance (given by the
GARCH prediction) constitute a probabilistic forecast (in the
application, we assume that the conditional distribution is the
normal distribution). Last, in the XGBoost/LEAR-CP model,
conformal prediction is applied to the mean-forecasts of the
models (see Sect. II-D). While sharing a basic building block
(the LEAR mean modeling), these approaches are fundamen-
tally different. The GARCH approach quantifies uncertainty
explicitly by modeling the conditional variance, whereas the
LEAR-QRA approach captures uncertainty implicitly using
an ensemble of predictors trained on different horizons. In
particular, short-term training windows can account for recent
increases in variance, as discussed in [2].
C. DEEP LEARNING-BASED CONCEPTS
As machine learning models are widely used today, we refrain
from providing a detailed introduction to deep learning and
machine learning models in general. Reader that are not
familiar with such concepts are referred to [21].
Lago et al. [2] show that simple two-layer feed-forward
neural networks are among the most effective deep learning
models for point forecasting. Building on this, Marcjasz et al.
[6] proposed the distributional deep neural network (DDNN),
a probabilistic extension that estimates the parameters of the
underlying price distribution rather than predicting electricity
prices directly. The model is trained by minimizing the nega-
tive log-likelihood loss (NLL):
LNLL =−
NX
i=1
logp(y i |x i;θ),(2)
wherex i andy i are the inputs and observed targets, and
p(yi |x i;θ)the probability assigned toy i by the distribution
predicted by the network with parametersθ. The output distri-
bution captures data uncertainty in the predictions [10]. To ad-
ditionally capture model uncertainty, various approaches can
be used, including ensemble methods, Bayesian approaches
such as Monte Carlo Dropout, and single deterministic meth-
ods such as Deep Evidential Regression [10].

1) Ensembles
The idea of ensemble methods is to combine different models,
i.e. their forecasts, to generate improved predictions, which
come at a cost, as multiple models must be calibrated and
maintained.
Ensembles also provide an intuitive way to measure model
uncertainty by capturing the variation in predictions across
the models. For NNs, it is essential to maximize the diversity
of the network’s behavior to obtain reliable uncertainty esti-
mates (while maintaining good predictive performance). This
can be done by training different architectures, training on
different subsets of the original dataset, or varying the initial
parameter set [22]. Lakshminarayanan et al. [23] found that
using different random initializations of the NN weights and
random shuffling suffices to create network diversity. To get
the predictive distribution, one has to aggregate the ensemble
models into a weighted mixture model:
p(y|x;θ) =
MX
j=1
wj p(y|x;θ j),(3)
using nonnegative weightsw 1, . . . ,wM that add up to one.
To calculate the quantileQ(p;θ) =F −1(p;θ)for a given
probabilityp∈[0,1],we solve the following equation:

2) Monte Carlo Dropout
While ensemble models train several NNs to capture model
uncertainty, Bayesian logic suggests an alternative approach
by interpreting individual weights as probabilistic variables.
The Monte Carlo (MC) dropout model is a widely used
example [24]. It differs from the DDNN by including dropout
layers after each hidden layer. These dropout layers remain
active during both training and inference. As a result, the
same input can produce different outputs in multiple forward
passes through the network. During inference, we performN
forward passes and aggregate the results using a uniformly
weighted mixture model. Quantiles are then obtained by solv-
ing Equation 4, equivalent to the ensemble approach.
3) Deep Evidential Regression
Deep evidential regression (DER) is a single deterministic
method, introduced by Amini et al. [25], where one evidential
deep neural network (EvDNN) predicts both the forecast and
its uncertainty. In contrast to a Bayesian method, priors are
placed directly over the parameters of the distribution instead
of the network weights. If a Gaussian distribution is assumed,
a Gaussian prior is placed on the mean and an inverse gamma
prior on the variance:
y∼ N(µ, σ 2),
withµ∼ N(γ, σ 2ν−1), σ 2 ∼Γ −1(α, β), (5)
whereγ∈R,ν >0,α >1, andβ >0. This
leads to a normal-inverse gamma distribution for the joint

p(µ, σ2) =p(µ)(σ 2):

D. MODEL-AGNOSTIC APPROACHES
Model-agnostic approaches do not require assumptions about
a specific probability distribution or regression model. In-
stead, they can be applied on top of any forecasting model.
Historical simulations are examples, as described in Section
II-B. Another example is Conformal Prediction [9]. Given a
trained model on historical data, PIs are constructed using
nonconformity scores, computed from the residuals of a dis-
tinct calibration set for each hour of the day. For each dayd

III. ELECTRICITY DATA
All data were retrieved from the SMARD platform
(smard.de), operated by the German Federal Network
Agency. For forecasting power prices, we consider not only
the price itself but also load forecasts and renewable energy
generation forecasts. Daily seasonality is captured using
weekday dummies. The dataset covers the period from 1
October 2018 to 30 November 2024. However, entire days
are regularly missing in the load forecast series for some
particular days. The total dataset has2,253daily entries,
out of which only65contain missing data. It turns out that
missing data does not correlate with any important events. All
but 8 were due to Austria leaving the joint bidding zone with
Germany and Luxemburg, which is a solitary event. The rows
with missing data are removed from the dataset, resulting
in a final dataset that begins on 12 October 2018. Daylight
saving time adjustments are handled by interpolating the
missing hour during the spring shift with the average of the
neighboring hours and resolving the duplicated hour during
the autumn shift by averaging the two values.
There may be strong correlation or even multicollinearity
in the features, which could potentially cause instability
in the predictors. However, since all models are subject to
regularization, such problems are automatically taken care
of.
The power prices we consider are hourly day-ahead prices
with physical delivery, traded on the European Power Ex-
change (EPEX SPOT). The day-ahead auction is held daily,
with price settlement taking place at noon for delivery on the
following day [6].
An overview of the dataset is provided in Fig. 1, which
shows several noteworthy characteristics. Negative prices ap-
pear regularly. However, the period between mid-2021 and
December 2022 stands out as an exception, with almost no
negative prices, comparatively high volatility, and consider-
ably large price spikes. Price spikes can also be observed
in other years and are due to the physical delivery of elec-
tricity, combined with the fact that, up to now, it cannot be
stored in large quantities in Germany. As a consequence, in
November 2024, when Germany experienced a period of low

wind and limited solar generation, together with insufficient
fossil power, this led to a price surge of more than 800 EUR
per MWh. In general, price properties vary considerably over
time, which is why we refrain from computing fundamental
statistical measures such as skewness, variance, or kurtosis.
Fig. 1 further supports the assumption of time-varying volatil-
ity.
Both renewable energy generation and load forecasts are
displayed in Fig. 2. Load exhibits clear annual seasonality,
with lower demand in summer than in winter. While over-
all load volumes remain relatively stable across years, the
structure within individual years is changing, though not to
the extent of power prices. Forecasted renewable generation
is increasing over time, consistent with infrastructure efforts
in Germany. At this level, no distinct seasonality is visible,
which may be explained by the negative correlation between
forecasted solar and wind generation.

IV. CASE STUDY
To evaluate whether incorporating model uncertainty into
deep learning models improves interval forecasts, we assess
eight augmentations of the deep distributional neural net-
work (DDNN) on the dataset described in Section III. These
include ensemble models of 5 and 10 DDNNs (Ens5 and
Ens10), MC Dropout models with 10 or 30 forward passes
(MCD10 and MCD30), and an evidential deep neural network
(EvDNN). Both ensembles and dropout models employ a
Gaussian mixture aggregation scheme. In addition, all point
forecasts (excluding Ens5 and MCD10) are combined with
conformal prediction (suffix "–CP"). The DDNN, which ac-
counts only for data uncertainty, serves as the baseline. For
comparison, we also consider statistical benchmarks: LEAR-
GARCH, LEAR-QRA, LEAR point forecasts with conformal
prediction (LEAR-CP), and a naive approach combined with
historical simulation based on the training and validation
datasets (Naive-HS train and Naive-HS val). In total, we eval-
uate 15 models. All of the models are implemented in the
Python framework and they are publicly available through a
Github repository1.
A. INPUT FEATURES AND PREPROCESSING
The following151features are used as inputs to our models:
•Day-ahead prices from the past three days and from the
same weekday of the previous week.
•Day-ahead forecasts of total load.
•Day-ahead forecasts of renewable energy generation.
•Weekday dummies, represented as binary vectors (e.g.,
[1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0] indicates Monday).
1Link to Python Code: Accessed on 1 Feb, 2026
Since the features have different scales, all151input fea-
tures and24output values are standardized using area hyper-
bolic sine variance stabilization transformation [26]. Finally,
the dataset is split into training, validation, and test sets. The
training set covers 12 October 2018 to 30 November 2022, the
validation set spans 1 December 2022 to 30 November 2023,
and the test set includes all days between 1 December 2023
and 30 November 2024.
B. MODEL CALIBRATION AND TRAINING
All deep learning models use the "He" initialization for the
hidden layers and the "Glorot" initialization for the output
layer. During training, early stopping is applied with a pa-
tience of 100 epochs, and the maximum number of training
epochs is set to 2000. The models are optimized using the
ADAM optimizer with a batch size of 32. To reduce over-
fitting, all models employ L 2 regularization. Additionally,
10 independent runs are performed for each model, and the
results are averaged. To ensure reproducibility, a fixed ran-
dom seed is used for each training run. During these runs,
the hyperparameters are fixed to the optimal ones, which are
determined before. For the MCD10 and MCD30 models, only
a single forward pass is performed during training, while
validation involves 10 and 30 forward passes, respectively.
To improve numerical stability during training, we follow the
approach of [27] and predict the logarithm of the variance,
logσ 2, instead of predicting the varianceσ 2 directly. For the
EvDNN, we similarly predictlogν,log(α−1), andlogβ
instead ofν,α, andβ, and for the DDNN we predictlogσ 2
in place ofσ 2.
For the LEAR model, we follow [3] and train for different
length of datasets, specifically 56, 84, 1092, and 1461 days
for 24 hour forecasting horizon. We average the results to
produce the final point forecast. Additionally, we employ a
rolling window scheme. The QRA and GARCH approaches
use the mean forecasts obtained from the LEAR model based
on the validation set. We fit 24 hourly GARCH models, each
trained only on data from its corresponding hour. For the naive
model, we use the previous day’s price as the mean forecast
for days during Tuesday and Friday, and prices from the
same day of the previous week to predict prices for Monday,
Saturday, and Sunday.
For conformal prediction, we use the validation samples as
a calibration set, following [9]. For each test daydand hourh,
we apply a rolling window of the most recent nonconformity
scores specific to that hour, ensuring that only scores from the
same hour across different days are used.
C. HYPERPARAMETER OPTIMIZATION
Before training, we performed hyperparameter optimization
using the tree-structured Parzen estimator, a Bayesian opti-
mization method implemented in the Optuna framework [28].
For the deep learning models, we optimized the learn-
ing rate, regularization parameters, dropout rate, and the
evidence regularization parameter, with their corresponding
search ranges listed in Table 4. We kept the network ar-
6 VOLUME 11, 2023
This article has been accepted for publication in IEEE Access. This is the author's version which has not been fully edited and 
content may change prior to final publication. Citation information: DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2026.3672716
This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 License. For more information, see https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

Lebedevet al.: Preparation of Papers for IEEE Access
chitecture fixed across all deep learning models to ensure
comparability and to focus the benchmark on differences in
uncertainty/interval prediction. Therefore, all deep learning
models use the same architecture with two hidden layers of
1,024 neurons each. The hidden layers use ReLU activation
functions, and the output layer uses a linear activation. Two-
layer feed-forward networks are commonly used as strong
baselines for day-ahead electricity price forecasting [29]. The
choice of 1,024 neurons per layer follows the upper end of
the width range considered in the extensive hyperparameter
search of [30]. All hyperparameters, except the dropout
rate, were sampled on a logarithmic scale. The optimization
process consisted of 200 trials. The validation loss was used
as the objective value for the tree-structured Parzen estimator
algorithm. In each trial for the NN models, three runs were
trained using the same hyperparameter values to reduce the
effect of randomness, and the average validation loss across
these three runs was then used as the objective value. Note
that once the optimal hyperparameters are found, the actual
training of ensembles of NNs is performed using these opti-
mal hyperparameters.
For the LEAR and XGBoost models, we optimized the
LASSO penalty parameter for LEAR as well as the XGBoost
hyperparameters described in Table 4 using only the specifi-
cation with the largest calibration window (1,461 days). The
optimization process likewise consisted of 200 trials, with
validation loss used as the objective. The resulting parameter
settings were applied across all forecasting horizons.

error (MAE) and the root mean square error (RMSE) are used,

We compare forecasting performances of models pairwise
using the Diebold-Mariano (DM) test for overall performance
comparison and the Giacomini-White (GW) test for condi-
tional comparisons, see [33] and [34] respectively, using the
CRPS as the loss function. For the mathematical formulation
of the DM test, please refer to Appendix B. Finally, we use
the probability integral transformation (PIT) as a diagnostic
tool to descriptively access the distributional fit of selected
models. To this end, we evaluate the predicted distribution
function for daydand hourh, ˆFd,h , at the observationp d,h . If
the predicted distribution is well calibrated, the transformed
variable, i.e. ˆFd,h(pd,h), ought to be standard uniformly dis-
tributed. In practice, the histogram of{ ˆFd,h(pd,h)}d=I for
some prediction intervalI, is inspected for deviations from
uniformity. Since most of our probabilistic predictions are
characterized by quantiles, we approximate the PIT-values by
interpolating between percentiles.
E. ERROR ANAL YSIS
We begin by evaluating the point prediction performance
of the models. According to Table 1, the XGBoost model
achieves the best overall point prediction performance, with
an MAE of12.020and an RMSE of20.534, outperforming
all other models. The performance of LEAR models are
significantly better than the deep learning models however
they are outperformed by the XGBoost models by a small
margin. As expected, the naive models yield significantly

higher errors compared to the NN-based and statistical ap-
proaches. Among the neural networks, the DDNN already
achieves a considerable reduction in MAE and RMSE relative
to the naive models. The ensemble models further improve
performance, reducing MAE and RMSE compared to the
DDNN. While increasing the number of models in the en-
semble brings only marginal performance improvements, it
noticeably reduces the standard deviation of the error metrics.
MC Dropout models lead to even greater improvements, with
reductions in MAE and RMSE of up to6.4% and4.9%
relative to the DDNN. The number of forward passes in the
MC Dropout models shows only a marginal positive effect on
performance. Notably, the EvDNN achieves the lowest MAE
among the neural models, with a7.4% reduction compared to
the DDNN.
When examining the interval forecasts, it becomes clear
that the EvDNN model struggles to capture uncertainty ac-
curately. It produces a relatively high MAACE of about44%
and the third-highest CRPS among all models. Similar to the
point forecasts, the DDNN model significantly improves the
probabilistic metrics compared to the naive baselines, and
both ensemble and MC Dropout extensions further enhance
performance. Specifically, they reduce the CRPS by about4%
and7%, respectively, compared to the DDNN. For MAACE,
these methods achieve notable improvements as well. The
ensemble reduces MAACE by3points (a49% improvement)
and MC Dropout by3.6points (a67% improvement), again
relative to the DDNN. Interestingly, increasing the number
of ensemble models has a strong impact on CRPS but little
effect on MAACE, while the opposite trend is observed with
the number of forward passes in the MC Dropout models.
Another point worth noting is the relatively high standard
deviation of MAACE produced by the DDNN, which is con-
siderably larger than that of the other models. The XGBoost-
GARCH model achieves the best overall forecasting perfor-
mance in terms of CRPS, with a CRPS of4.492, followed
closely by the XGBoost-CP model at4.493and the XGBoost-
QRA model at4.503. When assessing the uncertainty mea-
sure MAACE, the top-performing model is the GBoost-CP
with a value of1.090, followed by the LEAR-CP at1.305
and the MCD30-CP at1.736.

2 and Fig. 4. It should be noted that, of all the figures, there
are 10 models under consideration, whereas the tables in
this section include 15 models in total. Five models, namely
Naive-HStrain, Ens5, MCD10, EvDNN, and EvDNN-CP , are
not shown in Fig. 4 and Fig. 5, since we consider only one
better-performing model from each category, and the EvDNN
model struggles to capture uncertainty. The naive models
consistently produce PICP values higher than the expected
nominal coverage, indicating underconfident intervals. The
same holds for LEAR-GARCH and LEAR-CP . In contrast, all
deep learning models typically exhibit overconfidence in their
PIs, a limitation shared by XGBoost-GARCH and XGBoost-
QRA. However, these XGBoost variants demonstrate signif-
icant performance improvements specifically at confidence
levels exceeding 80%. Ultimately, XGBoost-CP proves to be
the most robust approach, outperforming all other models
by achieving the best overall Prediction Interval Coverage
Probability (PICP).
Both the ensemble and MC Dropout models show im-
proved PICP values compared to the DDNN, especially as
the confidence level increases. The greatest improvements are
observed around the90% confidence level. Up to the60%
confidence level, the performance of the ensemble and MC
Dropout models is quite similar. Moreover, both the ensemble
and MC Dropout models significantly reduce the standard
deviation of results across independent runs by about half
compared to the DDNN, indicating more stable performance.
After the60% confidence level, the DDNN-CP models sur-
pass both the ensemble and MC Dropout models. At about
the80% confidence level, the LEAR-QRA begins to surpass
the previous models, while the LEAR-CP achieves the best
overall coverage, as reflected in the MAACE metric.
As shown in Table 3 and Figure 5, the MPIW increases
almost linearly with the confidence level up to around the
70% confidence interval. As expected, the naive model pro-
duces significantly wider PIs on average, consistent with
its high PICP values. In contrast, the remaining approaches,
including the LEAR-based, XGBoost-based, and NN-based
methods, generate considerably narrower intervals, roughly
half the width of those from the naive model. The exception
is the EvDNN model, which produces very sharp but less
reliable PIs. Among the classical post-processing approaches,
the QRA variants (for both LEAR and XGBoost) are designed
to deliver sharp quantiles, and this is reflected in compara-
tively narrow PIs over low-to-mid confidence levels; in par-
ticular, LEAR-QRA consistently produces the narrowest PIs
across all confidence levels among the traditional and NN-
based models (excluding the EvDNN), with MPIW values

of17.88at50% confidence and about39.18at80%. At

where the highest gains in PICP are observed, the Ens10 and
MC30 models improve PICP by4.36and5.89percentage
points, respectively, in exchange for increases in MPIW by
4.14and2.63, reflecting the trade-off between interval width
and coverage. Between the two, MC Dropout performs better
overall. Additionally, we calculate the probability integral
transform (PIT) of the actual observations w.r.t. the predictive
distributions of the respective models. If a models probabilis-
tic forecast is well calibrated, the PIT-values follow a uniform
distribution. To assess this, we plot the histograms of the PIT-
values (Fig. 12 in the Appendix D) and inspect deviations
from uniformity. It can be observed that the XGBoost model
with conformal prediction uncertainty quantification is well
calibrated. The DDNN model suffers from probability mass
near the boundaries, i.e.0and1. This can be explained by the
model not being able to properly predict extreme events. The
Monte Carlo dropout approach to the DDNN model seems
to mitigate this problem at least for the upper boundary1.
Correcting the inflation near the boundary0is a potential
future research direction.
F. STATISTICAL TESTS
In this section we discuss the results of applying two standard
forecast comparison procedures: (a) the Diebold–Mariano
test (DM test), see [33], and (b) the Giacomini–White test
(GW test), see [34], for conditional predictive ability. In this
and in the following section, we leave out the following
five models from our analysis Naive-HS train, Ens5, MCD10,
EvDNN, and EvDNN-CP , since we only want to consider
well-performing models from each category.We choose a
significance level ofα= 0.05. We decide against multiple

1) Diebold-Mariano Test
Thep-values in the DM test show whether the two models
under consideration are significantly different in terms of
prediction accuracy. However, they do not provide any infor-
mation about models performance superiority. To extract this
information, one has to analyze the test statistic. The mathe-
matical form of the DM test and the table of the test statistic
are given in Appendix B in Table 8. Table 8 reports the
corresponding DM statisticsd i,j (based on CRPS loss), where
di,j <0meansM i attains lower average loss thanM j (row is
better),d i,j >0means the opposite (column is better),|d i,j|
quantifies the strength of the advantage, and values numeri-
cally near0indicate practical equivalence. In Fig. 6, we show
the pairwisep-values (row modelM i vs. column modelM j),
with significance level0.05. Entries whose numeric values on
the color bar are<0.05indicate that the observed difference
between the two models is statistically significant, whereas
largerp-values>0.05indicate no detectable difference. The
diagonal elements are left blank since models are not tested
against themselves.
Each model is compared with every other model across
10 independent runs. The results show that the three XG-
Boost–type models form a statistically tied top tier: XG-

Boost–GARCH, XGBoost–QRA, and XGBoost–CP perfor-
mances are mutually indistinguishable, with near-zero dif-
ferentials and non-rejections in all pairwise directions, while
LEAR variants being competitive to XGBoost variants. The
pairwise DM statistics given in Table 8 in Appendix D sup-
port this claim. For further clarity on thep-values, we also
provide their numerical values in Table 9 in the Appendix
D. However, each of these XGBoost models dominates every
other models, except the LEAR-CP and LEAR-QRA, by a
wide and statistically significant margin. All deep-learning
models (DDNN, Ens10, MCD30) and their conformal/MC
Dropout variants (DDNN-CP , Ens10-CP , MCD30-CP) are
statistically indistinguishable from one another atα= 0.05;
however, directional tendencies do exist as MCD30 seems to
be performing better, generally, although this difference is not
significant. Conformal and MC Dropout models do not yield
measurable gains (in terms of CRPS) over their corresponding
base models. Finally, every method strictly improves upon the
naive baseline.
In summary, (i) there is no single best model within the
XGBoost family, but together they form a statistically su-
perior performance frontier; (ii) deep-learning methods are
statistically tied with one another and uniformly inferior to
the XGBoost and LEAR models; and (iii) naive forecasting
is decisively outperformed by all other approaches.
2) Giacomi - White Test
The Giacomini–White (GW) test evaluates conditional pre-
dictive ability rather than only unconditional mean perfor-
mance. The key design choice in the GW framework is the
information set on which predictive ability is evaluated. This
is encoded through the instrument vector [c.f. Appendix C],

FIGURE 7.Heatmap of pairwise Giocami-White testp-values using CRPS
loss. Values below 0.05 mark significant differences in predictive
accuracy. Results are averaged over 10 independent runs, yielding 130
comparisons per model pair across runs.
which is required to be measurable with respect to the fore-
caster’s information available at a given time. The mathe-
matical description and the tables for the P-values and the
test statistic are given in the Appendix C and D respect-
fully. Taking the motivation from [26], we implement the
GW test and found that empirically, the GW statistics are
extremely large for most pairs, implying essentially zero p-
values under theχ 2
2 reference. For example,GW DDNN,Naive =
207.52corresponds to a p-value on the order of10 −46, and
GWXGBoost-GARCH,Naive = 710.53corresponds to a p-value on
the order of10 −155. This indicates overwhelming evidence
that the models differ in conditional predictive ability relative
to the naive baseline. Likewise, comparisons of the neu-
ral baselines against LEAR/XGBoost variants are associated
with very large GW statistics (typically>150and often
>200), again implying p-values effectively zero and con-
firming that these families are not conditionally equivalent.
The striking difference compared to the DM test appears
within the top-performing families. Although the DM statis-
tics between LEAR variants are near zero (suggesting practi-
cal equivalence in mean CRPS), the corresponding GW statis-
tics are not small. For example,GW LEAR-GARCH,LEAR-QRA =
151.41(p-value≈1.3×10 −33) indicates strong rejection of
conditional equality even when the unconditional mean gap
is negligible by DM. The same phenomenon is visible for
several other ‘‘close’’ model pairs:GWLEAR-GARCH,LEAR-CP =
6.65(p-value≈0.036) andGW XGBoost-CP,XGBoost-GARCH =
12.44(p-value≈0.002). These results mean that, under
zt = (1,d t), the loss differential does not behave like a
conditionally mean-zero martingale difference; rather, it ex-
hibits detectable temporal structure captured byd t (persis-
tence/reversal in relative performance), even when the aver-
age difference is small.
Hence, the GW test does not contradict the DM test; it
answers a stronger question: not only whether the average
CRPS values are equal, but also whether relative performance
is conditionally stable when conditioned on the most recent
loss differential. In our results, several model pairs that appear
practically tied in mean CRPS under DM nonetheless show
significant differences under GW, which is precisely the type
of conditional structure that the additional instrumentd t is
designed to detect.
G. TRADING STRATEGIES
A different angle to evaluate the goodness of fit of a specific
forecasting method is to integrate it into a trading strategy
and observe the financial success. We follow the suggestion
of [35] and aim to optimally control a battery storage system
based on interval forecasts of the German day-ahead power
price. Let the battery have a capacity ofB= 2MWhand a
charging/discharging efficiency ofξ= 90%. Each trading
dayd, withd= 1, . . . ,DandDbeing the number of trading
days, we pick an hourh buy for buying1MWhand another hour
hsell for selling it. We start with an initial charge ofB d =
1MWhon dayd= 1. Transaction costs are ignored.
We consider a quantile-based strategy that uses PIs gener-
ated by each of the methods tested in Section IV -E, as well as
the perfect foresight strategy, where we know the true prices,
as the profit’s upper boundary. The quantile-based strategy
works by setting limits, which are given by the PIs: the selling
price is equal to the lower boundary of the highest price’s PI

In Fig. 8, the total profits for all tested strategies are
shown depending on the chosen confidence level. We see
that each model’s total payoff peaks at a certain confidence
level, after which it declines, and this peak confidence level
differs by model. The NN-based model’s profit, for example,
culminates around50%, while the naive model peaks around
30%. For the LEAR-based models, the peak shifts to higher
confidence levels (around85% for LEAR-QRA and around
90% for LEAR-GARCH), indicating that these models can
remain profitable even when the strategy becomes more con-
servative. For the XGBoost family, the peak typically occurs
at medium confidence levels (roughly in the60–70% range),
with XGBoost-CP generally performing best among the XG-
Boost variants across a broad range of confidence levels.

The decline in total profit at higher confidence levels is
caused by the widening PIs, which lead to fewer trading
days identified as profitable and therefore fewer executed
trades, as shown in Fig. 9. This mechanism applies to the
XGBoost variants as well: at high confidence levels, the
intervals become wider, the trading conditions are satisfied
less frequently, and total profit drops even if the remaining
trades can be individually attractive.
Both the ensemble and MC Dropout models outperform the
DDNN model in terms of total profit at the90% confidence
level, despite having wider PIs as shown in Fig. 5. At the
70% confidence level, where the difference in total profit is
most significant, the ensemble model achieves a profit that
is3.7% higher, while the MC Dropout model achieves an
8.4% higher profit compared to the DDNN model. In the
same confidence region, the XGBoost models are competitive
with the NN-based approaches, and the conformalized variant
(XGBoost-CP) is typically the strongest within the XGBoost
group, reflecting the benefit of improved calibration for the
trading rule.
Notably, the LEAR-QRA model outperforms all other
models between confidence levels of approximately35% and
85%, until the PIs become too wide. Interestingly, below
35% and again between85% and95%, the LEAR-CP model
achieves the highest total profits, showing that calibration can
be especially valuable in the very aggressive (low confidence)
and very conservative (high confidence) regimes.
Fig. 10 shows the profit per transaction. The per-
transaction profit in quantile-based strategies tends to in-
crease with higher confidence levels. In contrast, the statis-
tical models show an initial decline up to around the50%
confidence interval, after which their profits begin to rise.
Interestingly, the LEAR-CP model remains relatively stable
up to around90%, before it also starts to increase.

After reaching the50% confidence level, the naive model
begins to outperform the others in terms of per-transaction
profit. This suggests that although it executes fewer trades, the
trades it does make are generally more profitable; however, its
profit curve starts to decline at the90% confidence level. The
XGBoost variants follow the same general logic of “fewer
but stronger” trades at high confidence levels: as confidence
increases, the strategy becomes more selective, which raises
profit per executed trade even though total profit can still fall
due to the reduced number of transactions.
Notably, the NN models and their CP counterparts exhibit
very similar per-transaction profits. A similar pattern is vis-
ible for XGBoost and its conformalized version: differences
in per-transaction profit are usually modest at medium con-
fidence levels, while at very high confidence levels the per-
transaction profit can rise sharply because only the most fa-
vorable opportunities remain tradable. Finally, the statistical
models demonstrate higher per-transaction profits than all
other models during the first half of the confidence level;
afterward, LEAR-GARCH and LEAR-QRA tend toward the
performance of the other models, while LEAR-CP remains
significantly lower than the rest.
The tables for Fig. 8, Fig. 9, and Fig. 10, along with
their corresponding plots against PICP , can be found in Ap-
pendix D.
V. DISCUSSION AND CRITICAL REFLECTION
In general, it shows that there is no superior method that
performs best across all error measures. However, there is a
certain tendency towards XGBoost and LEAR-based models,
which show better performance in the presence of state-of-
the-art deep learning benchmarks, despite being much sim-
pler and requiring considerably less computational power.
This indicates, at least given the setup of this case study,
that the additional complexity of deep learning models is not
paying off.
Our case study shows that the XGBoost-CP model has,
on average, the most reliable PIs across all models, with a
MAACE of1.090, whereas the best deep learning model,
MC Dropout, achieves a MAACE of1.735. In contrast, the
XGBoost-QRA and XGBoost-GARCH variants are notice-
ably less reliable in terms of MAACE, illustrating that strong
point prediction alone does not guarantee well-calibrated in-
tervals unless the uncertainty layer is appropriate.
At a confidence level of around85%and higher, the LEAR-
QRA starts to outperform the MD model, achieving a better
PICP . The evidential neural network failed to capture the
uncertainty. One possible reason could be the zero-gradient
problem for evidential regression models; see [36] for more
information. The LEAR-GARCH also had difficulties in pro-
viding reliable PIs, as did the naive approach; and a similar
limitation is visible for the XGBoost-GARCH construction,
whose uncertainty is entirely driven by residual dynamics
and the chosen parametric distributional assumption. The
problem is that these approaches rely heavily on how rep-
resentative the historical residual period is for the current
regime and on whether the assumed conditional distribution
is appropriate. The superior performance of the XGBoost and
LEAR-based models may be explained by the fact that they
are refitted for every prediction. This is only possible because
of the relatively low computational cost.
A possible reason could be the use of the rolling window
scheme in contrast to the NN models, where the training
data is fixed. In particular, both LEAR and XGBoost can
be retrained frequently with updated windows, which allows
them to adapt to changing levels of volatility and changing
feature relevance; in contrast, the NN models in our setup are
trained once on a fixed dataset and then evaluated, making
them more exposed to nonstationarity and domain shifts un-
less additional adaptation mechanisms are introduced.
Our study indicates that quantifying both data and model
uncertainty, particularly for deep learning models, pays off.
In particular, ensemble-based methods and MC Dropout im-
prove robustness and stability relative to a single DDNN, and
often also improve point accuracy. Interestingly, evidential
deep neural networks can achieve strong point accuracy but
still generate less reliable PIs compared to their benchmarks.
We find that improvements in reliability come at the cost
of wider PIs, i.e., reduced sharpness. From the perspective
of the XGBoost family, this trade-off appears in a different
form: XGBoost-QRA prioritizes sharpness by learning quan-
tiles directly, XGBoost-GARCH prioritizes a volatility-based
parametric uncertainty model, and XGBoost-CP prioritizes
calibration through empirical error distributions; the empir-
ical results indicate that the calibration-oriented approach is
the most robust here.
Interestingly, incorporating model uncertainty into DDNN
models also helps improve their point forecasts. This is due
14 VOLUME 11, 2023
This article has been accepted for publication in IEEE Access. This is the author's version which has not been fully edited and 
content may change prior to final publication. Citation information: DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2026.3672716
This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 License. For more information, see https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

Lebedevet al.: Preparation of Papers for IEEE Access
to the procedures to quantify and estimate model uncertainty,
and not due to modeling uncertainty itself.
In terms of economic benefits, good performance in in-
terval forecasting is no guarantee of actual profit in daily
trading. Rather, the confidence level acts as a decision knob:
as predicted limits become more conservative, the strategy
becomes more selective, which typically reduces the number
of trades but can increase per-transaction profit.
Eventually, there are a few limitations of the tested models
that need to be mentioned. For example, we see that it pays
off to use ensemble models for generating PIs. However,
the choice of the required hyperparameters is rather tricky.
Ensemble forecasting requires specifying the number of en-
semble members, which is difficult to determine. Addition-
ally, the composition of these members is significant. Weak
members can harm overall performance, and equal-weight
aggregation might be suboptimal.
In the statistical models, we implemented a rolling window
approach for calibrating the parameters. Although this is ben-
eficial in many situations, it causes problems during structural
breaks. Moreover, the window size needs to be chosen before-
hand, and this choice is always somewhat arbitrary. Statistical
models are lighter and interpretable but can be brittle under
regime shifts and heavy tails if distributional assumptions
are too restrictive. ML models are adaptive but need careful
regularization and calibration to avoid over- or underconfi-
dence. Rather than choosing one, the evidence suggests a
hybrid path: use LEAR-type models for baseline calibration
and coverage control, use XGBoost-type models to capture
nonlinear feature effects efficiently, and combine them with
explicit calibration layers (such as CP) when diagnostic plots
indicate systematic miscalibration.
In this study, Gaussian innovations were used for compa-
rability. Moreover, a natural extension is to test heavy-tailed
and skewed families (Student-t, skew-t, generalized error,
generalized hyperbolic or JSU) within LEAR-GARCH. The
same extension is relevant for the residual-based XGBoost-
GARCH construction: if residuals are heavy-tailed or skewed,
a Gaussian assumption can distort tail quantiles and thereby
coverage at high nominal levels. This could retain the cali-
bration advantages while improving tail coverage, again pro-
viding a way to strengthen statistical/parametric uncertainty
layers without diminishing the role of ML.
Several mechanisms identified in this study are not
country-specific but are shared by markets with high shares
of variable renewable energy. However, generalizing our find-
ings is hard. Whether our results can be transferred depends
on various factors. Regulation, which for example might in-
hibit or ease market access, varies across countries. Systems
with an equal or even larger share of renewable power such
as Norway) may actually exhibit weaker price volatility as
their hydro generation capacities function as buffer storages.
Conversely, systems with high shares of non-dispatchable
renewables but limited storage are likely to experience dy-
namics closer to those observed in Germany. The French
market, still dominted by nuclear power, may show similar
price patterns as, lately, price effects are often due to German
power surplus supply or additional power demand.
VI. CONCLUSION
In this article, we test a wide range of methods on their
capability to produce reliable interval forecasts for hourly
power prices. In this context, we analyze whether forecasting
accuracy improves if model and data uncertainty are explicitly
considered using an adequate model, such as a Bayesian
approach. An extensive model comparison based on various
goodness-of-fit measures is performed, whereby both statis-
tical and machine learning models are tested. It shows that
there is no model that performs best across all measures.
Moreover, having also considered economic implications in
the context of a trading scheme, we see that increasing the
precision of interval forecasts does not necessarily increase
profits. With regard to prediction intervals, it pays off to ac-
count for uncertainty, and a combined focus on both aleatoric
and epistemic uncertainty is beneficial for neural approaches.
Ensemble models help to reduce both MAE and RMSE com-
pared to a single DDNN and also stabilize results across
runs. However, they are outperformed by classical baselines
in this case study, where refitting and calibration play a
central role. In particular, statistical LEAR models remain
highly competitive, and combining LEAR with a GARCH
volatility component proves to be fairly reliable for interval
construction. Beyond LEAR, the tree-based XGBoost family
provides a strong ‘‘middle ground’’ between linear statisti-
cal models and deep neural networks: it captures nonlinear
feature interactions with modest training cost, and its perfor-
mance depends crucially on the uncertainty layer applied on
top of the mean model. In terms of distributional accuracy,
the residual-based XGBoost–GARCH variant achieves the
best overall CRPS in our study, and XGBoost–QRA yields
similarly competitive CRPS values. In terms of reliability,
however, the conformalized variant XGBoost–CP is the most
robust approach, achieving the lowest MAACE and strong
coverage behavior across nominal levels. This highlights that,
even with a strong nonlinear mean predictor, well-calibrated
intervals are not automatic; rather, calibration-oriented pro-
cedures such as conformal prediction can be decisive for
producing reliable uncertainty estimates. From a statistical
standpoint, the strength of the LEAR family is calibration.
Their interval systems are directly tied to quantile/expectile
targets, which often translates into well-behaved Probability
Integral Transform (PIT) diagnostics and reliable Coverage
vs. Nominal (CvN) curves. A constructive next step, without
undermining ML, would be to use LEAR-based forecast dis-
tributions as calibration anchors for neural outputs (e.g., post-
hoc quantile mapping or conformalized residuals). Eventu-
ally, we are aware of a few limitations of our study and paths
for future research. First, only the German power market is
tested, and it remains to be verified how the models perform
on other markets. With regard to machine learning models,
we could test hybrid uncertainty quantification methods, i.e.,
we could try to combine complementary methods in order
VOLUME 11, 2023 15
This article has been accepted for publication in IEEE Access. This is the author's version which has not been fully edited and 
content may change prior to final publication. Citation information: DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2026.3672716
This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 License. For more information, see https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

Lebedevet al.: Preparation of Papers for IEEE Access
to capture both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty. A nat-
ural choice would be to create ensembles of MC Dropout
models. Other hybrid approaches can be a combination of
complementary methods to improve uncertainty estimation.
For instance, we can combine distributional models with
conformal calibration, which can fix miscalibration while
preserving distribution shape, and deep ensembles combined
with conformal prediction to capture model uncertainty while
ensuring valid coverage. Post-hoc calibration is not yet fully
explored [37]. Other methods, such as adaptive ensemble
sizing and performance-based ensemble member selection,
might also help to improve PIs. Furthermore, more complex
distribution families, such as the generalized hyperbolic dis-
tribution for modeling randomness, could be explored, or
alternatively, distribution-free approaches. Eventually, con-
sidering the comparably poor financial performance of the
tested complex models, one needs to explore new possibilities
that arise from the increasing availability of storage capacity
on the German market. Here, uncertainty quantification could
be more beneficial than in the currently tested scenario.

B. THE DIEBOLD-MARIANO TEST
The Diebold-Mariano (DM) test is designed as follows: Let
e1t ande 2t denote the forecast errors of Model 1 and Model
2, respectively, at timet. To quantify the loss associated
with these errors, a loss functiong(·)is employed. Common
choices forg(·)include the squared error loss,g(e t) =e 2
t ,
or the absolute error loss,g(e t) =|e t |. The differential loss
at timetis then defined asd t =g(e 1t)−g(e 2t). The null
hypothesis (H 0) of the DM test posits that the two forecasts
exhibit identical accuracy, implying that the expected value
of the loss differential is zero:
H0 :E[d t] = 0
The alternative hypothesis (H 1) asserts that the forecasting
accuracies are distinct:
H1 :E[d t]̸= 0
The DM test statistic is constructed as:
DM=
¯dq
cV ar(¯d)
where ¯d= 1
T
PT
t=1 dt represents the sample mean of the loss
differential overTobservations, and cV ar(¯d)is a consistent
estimator of the variance of ¯d. This variance estimator is
crucial, as it accounts for potential serial correlation and
heteroskedasticity inherent in the loss differential seriesd t .
Under the null hypothesis, the DM test statistic asymptot-
ically follows a standard normal distribution, i.e.,DM∼
N(0,1). Effective application of the DM test for forecast
accuracy assessment necessitates several key prerequisites.
First, accurate computation of forecast errors for each model
is required, typically defined as the difference between the
observed value and the forecasted value. Second, a clearly
defined and appropriate loss function must be specified to
quantify the cost of forecasting errors in a manner relevant to
the specific application, as the selection of the loss function
directly impacts the interpretation of "accuracy." Third, as
an asymptotic test, the DM test relies on a sufficiently large
sample size (T) to ensure that the DM test statistic converges
to its asymptotic normal distribution, thereby validating the
statistical inference. Finally, while the original formulation
assumed covariance stationarity of the loss differential series
(dt ), modern extensions of the DM test can accommodate
non-stationary series, enhancing its applicability to a broader
range of time series data. Thep-value derived from the DM
test statistic serves as the basis for inference. Ap-value below
a pre-specified significance level (α, commonly 0.05) leads
to the rejection ofH 0, indicating a statistically significant
difference in forecasting accuracy between the two models.
C. GW TEST
The Giacomini–White (GW) test evaluates conditional pre-
dictive ability. Letℓ i,t andℓ j,t denote the CRPS losses of
modelsM i andM j at timet, and define the loss differential
as
dt =ℓ i,t −ℓ j,t .(21)
The key design choice in the GW framework is the infor-
mation set on which predictive ability is evaluated. This is
encoded through the instrument vectorz t , which is required
to be measurable with respect to the forecaster’s information
available at timet(i.e., before observingd t+1 ).
zt = (1,d t),(22)
and a one-step alignment(τ= 1). This choice has two
motivations. First, the constant instrument1ensures that the
GW null includes the unconditional equal-loss restriction as
a component. Indeed, ifE[z t dt+1] = 0holds forz t ≡1, then
E[dt+1] = 0, meaning there is no average CRPS advantage
between the two models.
Second, the lagged loss differentiald t is included to test for
state dependence in relative performance. Electricity prices
and their forecast errors are well known to exhibit strong tem-
poral dependence and regime-like behavior; consequently, it
is plausible that the model that ‘‘wins’’ today (lower loss)
tends to keep winning tomorrow (persistence), or that relative
performance alternates (mean reversion). The instrumentd t
provides a minimal way to detect such effects: ifd t contains
predictive information aboutd t+1 , then the relative perfor-
mance of the two models is not conditionally stable over
time. In other words,z t = (1,d t)tests whether the sign and
magnitude of the most recent advantage is informative for the
next period.
With this instrument choice, the GW null hypothesis is
H GW
0 :E[z t dt+1] = 0,(23)
18 VOLUME 11, 2023
This article has been accepted for publication in IEEE Access. This is the author's version which has not been fully edited and 
content may change prior to final publication. Citation information: DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2026.3672716
This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 License. For more information, see https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

Lebedevet al.: Preparation of Papers for IEEE Access
which jointly imposes (i)E[d t+1] = 0(no mean CRPS ad-
vantage) and (ii)E[d t dt+1] = 0(no predictability/persistence
in the loss differential from one period to the next).
The GW test yields a nonnegative Wald statisticGW i,j and
a p-value computed from aχ 2
q reference distribution with
q= dim(z t) = 2. We report the mean GW statistics in
Table 10 and the corresponding p-values in Table 11. Small
p-values (belowα= 0.05) indicate rejection of equal condi-
tional predictive ability. Importantly, because the statistic is
quadratic, it is symmetric in the model pair(GW i,j =GW j,i);
therefore, the GW statistic (and the two-sided GW p-value)
quantify whether two models differ, but do not encode which
model is better. Direction must be inferred from the sign of
¯d(equivalently, from the sign of the DM statistic reported in
Table 8).

indicate stronger evidence against equal conditional predictive ability (with instrumentsz t = (1,d t )), but the statistic itself does not encode directional
superiority.
